items.title: Branford Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: When the big bands died away, and the small groups took over, guys like Benny Carter stayed bitter and pissed off.

ctx.x: Coleman Hawkins had that kind of…. Younger musicians had that kind of reverence for him. Sonny Rollins is, to this day, still in awe of Coleman Hawkins. Coleman had that thing…. There’s a great recording of Coleman Hawkins toward the end of his life doing this record. It’s not a very good record. It’s a combination of strings and big band. It’s called “The Hawk Flies High in the Land of Hi-Fi.” They were doing these hi-fi records. MRC was doing these records and that was the thing. Cannonball Adderley in hi-fi,…

know, here is the guy who was playing in the twenties, when Charlie Parker, learning how to play like him, and then he’s - I don’t know how old he was, he was probably in his sixties – he’s playing like Bird. Like, just to humble yourself to that degree, to go from being the master to the student, is some of the most inspiring stuff that I have ever heard. And I can understand why Sonny revered him so much. Cause Hawk was always trying to get to the next thing. When the big bands died away, and the small groups…

Let’s talk about Coleman Hawkins. You know, he truly to me, there are very few, there’s a finite few people who continue to progress and, as you call it, seeker. Coleman Hawkins 1948 unaccompanied tenor sax solo.
